newsitem.title: FRANCE: Guillen, Bernard may be named to BoF Council - paper.
newsitem.headline: Guillen, Bernard may be named to BoF Council - paper.

text.p: The French government is likely to appoint Pierre Guillen, ex-head of the CNPF employers' group and Jean-Rene Bernard, former deputy governor of property lender Credit Foncier, on Friday to the Bank of France's policy-making body, French newspapers Liberation and Figaro reported.
But another newspaper Les Echos said current council member Jean Boissanat, an ex-journalist, could be reappointed to the nine-member council.
Officials at President Jacques Chirac's office have refused all comment on the appointments.

"Jacques Chirac was determined last night to appoint to the monetary policy council of the bank two men in whom he has full confidence -- Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard," Liberation said. But it said it did not rule out "last minute changes."
Les Echos said that, "last night three candidates were clear front-runners" -- Boissonnat, Guillen and Bernard.
The appointments are being closely watched by financial markets for any sign of a softening in the Bank's traditionally cautious approach to monetary easing.

The mandates of Boissonnat and former banker Bruno de Maulde expire next week. The government is expected to make its announcement on the makeup of the council later this morning after a regular cabinet meeting.
In an interview with Reuters last month Guillen said he was "radically against" devaluing the franc, but as an industrialist would have liked to have seen rates come down faster.

Bernard, whose son-in-law is deputy secretary-general in Chirac's office, is not thought to have very strong convictions on monetary policy. But he is close to Chirac and would be expected to follow the president's lead on policy.

Boissonnat and de Maulde are believed to be part of a six to three majority backing the existing policy of maintaining French interest rates slightly above those in Germany to protect the stability of the franc against the mark.

Two others members have argued publicly that France should cut rates without waiting for German easing to revive the economy and help bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment. A third member is believed to share that view.
The replacement of Boissonnat and de Maulde by two more dovish members could tip the balance in their favour.

Sources had said previously that Chirac had intervened personally to get Guillen and Bernard on the list of six nominees proposed by the heads of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the Economic and Social Council.

Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet, mindful of a 1993 attempt to bring French rates below German rates which ended in a franc crisis, is believed to oppose trying to do this again as long as the franc is below its European Exchange Rate Mechanism central rate of 3.35 per mark.
The franc was trading on Friday at 3.3740/43 per mark, down from its level late Thursday of 3.3712 3.3720/24.

Whatever the decision, economists said Chirac, who has repeatedly stated his commitment to a stable currency, is unlikely to do anything to endanger the franc-mark link, the cornerstone of the future European single currency.
They said if Chirac named Guillen and Bernard, it would probably be on the understanding no risks were to be taken with the franc.
The nomination of Guillen and Bernard, and ousting of Boissonnat, a vocal supporter of the stable franc policy, would nonetheless give Chirac big leverage over the Bank of France.

The other candidates on the list of nominees are diplomat Pierre Achard, Alain Prate, former vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB), and Robert Pelletier, former managing director of the Association of Credit Establishments (Afec), sources close to the nomination process have said.
